name: Mobile Location Data
title: Mobile Location Data
answer: Mobile location data is the record of where a phone has been, inferred from signals such as GPS, Wi-Fi connections and cell tower handoffs. In alternative data it is bought and sold as a panel: a large set of devices, each with a timestamped trail of visits, stripped of names but often carrying a persistent identifier. Buyers use it to estimate foot traffic, store visits, commute patterns and catchment areas for companies that do not publish such figures. It sits alongside card transaction panels and web scraping as one of the main ways investors and analysts try to see economic activity before it appears in filings.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Mobile location data is the record of where a phone has been, inferred from signals such as GPS, Wi-Fi connections and cell tower handoffs. In alternative data it is bought and sold as a panel: a large set of devices, each with a timestamped trail of visits, stripped of names but often carrying a persistent identifier. Buyers use it to estimate foot traffic, store visits, commute patterns and catchment areas for companies that do not publish such figures. It sits alongside card transaction panels and web scraping as one of the main ways investors and analysts try to see economic activity before it appears in filings.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The raw material comes from mobile apps that collect location with user consent, from software development kits embedded in those apps, and from carriers or bidstream sources. Aggregators clean the pings, snap them to points of interest, and resell the result as files or through a dashboard or API. Storage and processing are ordinary cloud infrastructure, with geospatial databases and columnar stores handling billions of rows. The heavy engineering is in device stitching, deduplication and matching coordinates to a stable list of venues.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Analysts start by defining a geography and a set of places, then count unique devices seen there over a period. They weight the panel to match known totals, such as census population or a retailer's disclosed store count, because no panel covers everyone. From there they build indices of visits, dwell time and trade area overlap, and compare them against company reports or card data. Machine learning enters mainly in classification and matching: separating home from work locations, detecting visits versus pass-throughs, and imputing missing pings. Results are usually presented as relative change rather than absolute revenue.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main risks are consent, re-identification and resale without clear permission, which have drawn regulatory attention in several jurisdictions and a run of privacy litigation. Provenance matters: buyers want to know which apps supplied the data, what notice users saw, and whether identifiers were hashed or rotated. Contracts typically restrict use, forbid attempts to identify individuals, and set retention limits.Practitioners treat documentation of source and consent as part of the product, not an afterthought.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Regulatory pressure and platform changes are pushing the industry toward aggregated, less granular products and toward panels built on explicit opt-in. On-device processing and differential privacy are being tested as ways to keep utility while reducing exposure. Demand is likely to stay strong for foot traffic and geospatial signals, but the edge will go to vendors who can document consent and defend their panel against bias. Expect consolidation among suppliers and closer scrutiny of how location panels are weighted and validated.
